paragraphs: Friend, here's what I hear in this passage. Paul is full of big plans: Spain, Rome, Jerusalem. But look at who gets the credit. He says he will not presume to speak of anything except "what Christ has accomplished through me" (Romans 15:18). He calls his work a gift of grace from God (Romans 15:15). The best workers I know are the ones who say, "I just showed up, and HE did the rest."

Now look at how Paul treats the believers in Rome. He's convinced they are "full of goodness, brimming with knowledge, and able to instruct one another" (Romans 15:14). Then he writes boldly anyway, as a reminder. I think that's a picture of how God's people help each other. Nobody is too wise to be reminded, and nobody is too small to be trusted with the truth. Paul also asks them to "join me in my struggle by praying to God for me" (Romans 15:30). Even an apostle asks for prayer, so I'm not too proud to ask either.

And the plans? They're held loosely, friend. Paul hopes to see Rome, but he says "by God's will" he may come with joy (Romans 15:32). He stops to carry a gift to the poor saints in Jerusalem before he chases his own dream (Romans 15:25-27). So here's the takeaway, baker: work hard, give gladly, pray for each other, and let God hold the calendar. Then you can end the day like Paul: "The God of peace be with all of you. Amen." (Romans 15:33)
